name: Old Kingdom of Egypt
info: The first great age of pharaonic Egypt, from the Third to the Sixth Dynasty, when god-kings ruling from Memphis raised the Step Pyramid and the pyramids of Giza and sent ships to Lebanon and Punt.

facts.founder: Djoser, first king of the Third Dynasty
facts.predecessor: The Early Dynastic Period, whose last king was related to the first two kings of the Old Kingdom
facts.successor: The First Intermediate Period from the Seventh Dynasty; the hereditary nomarchs' local dynasties

t: Under Sneferu, Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure of the Fourth Dynasty (2613–2494 BCE) the art of pyramid-building was perfected and the pyramids of Giza were raised.
The king, not yet called pharaoh, was held to be the incarnation of Horus, a living god who ruled absolutely and could demand the services and wealth of his subjects.
In the Sixth Dynasty power passed to hereditary nomarchs, and a drought between 2200 and 2150 BCE that stopped the Nile flood brought famine and the kingdom's collapse.
dyk: Old Kingdom shipbuilders used neither treenails nor metal fasteners: planks and superstructure were tightly tied and bound together with rope, and such ships sailed the length of the Red Sea to Punt.
ev: The Third Dynasty begins; its first king Djoser orders the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the work of his vizier Imhotep.
Sneferu founds the Fourth Dynasty, holds territory from Libya to Sinai and Nubia, and builds the Meidum, Bent and Red Pyramids.
Khufu commissions the Great Pyramid of Giza, in which the fully developed pyramid style is reached.
Userkaf founds the Fifth Dynasty, marked by the growing cult of Ra and the sun temples of Abusir.
Unas, the last king of the Fifth Dynasty, has the Pyramid Texts inscribed in his pyramid, the earliest ruler to do so.
The canal to Lake Moeris is dug, among the very large works of Nile flood control.
Pepi II begins his long reign (2278–2214 BCE), during which internal disorder sets in.
The Sixth Dynasty ends; drought, famine and civil war open the First Intermediate Period.

sections.foundation:
The Old Kingdom is the name Egyptologists give to the period from the Third to the Sixth Dynasty, 2686–2181 BCE, the first of three 'Kingdom' periods that mark the high points of civilisation in the lower Nile valley. The break with the Early Dynastic Period is not dynastic: the last king of that age was related to the first two kings of the Old Kingdom, and the royal residence stayed at Ineb-Hedj, the Egyptian name for Memphis. What justifies the division is the revolutionary change in architecture and the effects that large-scale building had on Egyptian society and its economy.

The first king of the Old Kingdom was Djoser of the Third Dynasty, who ruled some time between 2691 and 2625 BCE and ordered a pyramid, the Step Pyramid, in the necropolis of Memphis at Saqqara. His vizier and architect Imhotep is credited with the development of building in stone and with the conception of the step pyramid as a form, and a new era of building began. In this age the formerly independent states of Egypt became nomes under the king's rule, their former rulers forced to serve as governors or work in tax collection. Egyptians believed the king to be the incarnation of Horus, linking the human and spiritual worlds, and saw the universe as working in cycles that the king on earth laboured to keep stable. Information from the Fourth to the Sixth Dynasties is scarce, and the history of the era is literally 'written in stone', built from the monuments and their inscriptions.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Old Kingdom's economy turned on the Nile and on the king's command of labour and goods. The pyramids and their complexes were the largest works of the age; Sneferu used more stones than any other pharaoh, and the canal to Lake Moeris, dug around 2300 BCE, was likely also the source of water to the Giza pyramid complex centuries earlier. Egypt's growing appetite for ebony, incense such as myrrh and frankincense, gold, copper and other useful metals drove the building of ships fit for the open sea. Egyptians traded with Lebanon for cedar and sailed the length of the Red Sea to the Kingdom of Punt, in modern Eritrea, for ebony, ivory and aromatic resins; Sahure of the Fifth Dynasty commanded an expedition there. The shipwrights used no pegs or metal fasteners but bound planks and superstructure tightly together with rope. There was also direct trade with the Aegean and Anatolia.

The rulers of the Fifth Dynasty sent expeditions to the stone quarries and gold mines of Nubia and the mines of Sinai, and the Sixth Dynasty's peak under Pepi I and Merenre I brought flourishing trade and several mining and quarrying expeditions. Art served religion and ideology rather than enjoyment, and its workshops produced sculpture in hard stones, gneiss, graywacke, schist and granite, whose colours carried meaning: black for the soil after the Nile flood, green for vegetation and rebirth, red for the sun, white for purity.
sections.military:
The Old Kingdom's wars were campaigns of expansion and extraction on Egypt's frontiers rather than struggles for survival. Sneferu, first king of the Fourth Dynasty, held territory from ancient Libya in the west to the Sinai Peninsula in the east and to Nubia in the south, and founded a settlement at Buhen in Nubia that lasted two centuries. Under his successors there were military expeditions into Canaan and Nubia, and Egyptian influence reached up the Nile into what is now Sudan. The Fifth Dynasty's inscriptions and reliefs refer to and depict campaigns in Nubia and Asia alongside its expeditions to the quarries and mines of Nubia and Sinai.

The Sixth Dynasty was the most aggressive. Pepi I's reign was marked by aggressive expansion into Nubia, and at least five military expeditions were sent into Canaan; Merenre was active in Nubia too and sent officials to maintain Egyptian rule there from the northern border to the region south of the third cataract. These major military campaigns, with flourishing trade and mining, mark the dynasty's peak. The jubilee run, a royal rite established in the Old Kingdom, had the king run around markers that stood for the borders of Egypt, a display of the vigour that qualified him to go on ruling. The internal security that marked the whole period broke down only at its end, when the long reign of Pepi II gave way to succession struggles and the country slipped into civil wars within decades of his death.
sections.governance:
During the Old Kingdom the King of Egypt, not called pharaoh until the New Kingdom, became a living god who ruled absolutely and could demand the services and wealth of his subjects. He was the incarnation of Horus, and the stability of the cosmic cycles depended on him. The formerly independent states of the valley were reduced to nomes under his rule, their old rulers made governors or tax collectors, and the royal residence remained at Memphis. The Fourth Dynasty (2613–2494 BCE) was the zenith of royal power: Sneferu, then his son Khufu (2589–2566 BCE), whose sons Djedefre and Khafre may have quarrelled, then Menkaure, Shepseskaf and perhaps Djedefptah.

The Fifth Dynasty (2494–2345 BCE), from Userkaf, was marked by the growing importance of the cult of the sun god Ra, so that fewer efforts went to pyramid complexes and more to the sun temples of Abusir. Neferirkare Kakai (2475–2455 BCE) introduced the prenomen into the royal titulary, Nyuserre Ini (2445–2421 BCE) built extensively at Abusir and restarted royal activity at Giza, and Unas (2375–2345 BCE) was the earliest ruler to have the Pyramid Texts inscribed in his pyramid. Under the Sixth Dynasty (2345–2181 BCE) the king's power gradually weakened in favour of powerful nomarchs, the regional governors, who no longer belonged to the royal family; their charge became hereditary, creating local dynasties largely independent of the central authority.
sections.impact:
Egypt attained its first sustained peak of civilisation in the Old Kingdom, the 'Age of the Pyramids', and later Egyptians looked back on it as a golden age, a grandiose height to which all future kingdoms aspired. Its monuments defined Egypt for the world: the Step Pyramid of Saqqara, Sneferu's three pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur, the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza, with which the fully developed pyramid style was reached, Khafre's second pyramid and, in traditional thinking, the Great Sphinx of Giza, and Menkaure's, the smallest of the three great pyramids. The Pyramid Texts first inscribed under Unas are the earliest of their kind.

The Old Kingdom fixed the conventions of Egyptian art for the rest of its history. Frontality, composite composition and the hierarchy of scale, begun in the Early Dynastic Period and solidified now, made figures axial, symmetrical, proportional and reproducible, the head and legs in profile with the torso to the front, the king larger than all but the gods; male figures of the age have broad shoulders and long, muscled torsos, and the king was shown young and vital. Beyond the valley, the Old Kingdom's ships opened the Red Sea route to Punt and the sea route to Lebanon's cedar, its settlement at Buhen and its campaigns carried Egyptian rule deep into Nubia, and its trade reached the Aegean and Anatolia.
sections.decline:
The Old Kingdom ended from within and from the sky. During the Sixth Dynasty the power of the pharaoh gradually weakened in favour of the nomarchs, whose offices became hereditary and whose local dynasties grew largely independent of Memphis. Internal disorders set in during the incredibly long reign of Pepi II (2278–2214 BCE) towards the dynasty's end; his death, certainly well after that of his intended heirs, may have set off succession struggles, and the country slipped into civil wars within decades of his reign's close.

The final blow was the drought of the 22nd century BCE, a drastic fall in rainfall that for at least some years between 2200 and 2150 BCE prevented the normal flooding of the Nile. Whatever its cause, the collapse was followed by decades of famine and strife, the period of disunity and relative cultural decline that Egyptologists call the First Intermediate Period, beginning with the Seventh Dynasty; the tomb inscription of Ankhtifi, a nomarch of its early years, describes the pitiful state of the country when famine stalked the land. Some Egyptologists count the Seventh and Eighth Dynasties, still administered from Memphis, as the Old Kingdom's last phase. What survived was the memory of a golden age and its stone: the pyramids and their temples, the sculpture in granite and graywacke, the art whose conventions endured to the end of pharaonic Egypt, and the Pyramid Texts.

summary: The Old Kingdom of Egypt (2686–2181 BCE), ruled from Memphis by kings held to be living gods, raised the Step Pyramid and the pyramids of Giza, traded to Lebanon and Punt and campaigned in Nubia and Canaan, until hereditary nomarchs, the long reign of Pepi II and the drought of 2200–2150 BCE brought famine and collapse.

Mark Lehner, The Complete Pyramids (Thames & Hudson, 1997)
Jaromír Málek and Werner Forman, In the Shadow of the Pyramids: Egypt during the Old Kingdom (University of Oklahoma Press, 1986)
Naguib Kanawati, Governmental Reforms in Old Kingdom Egypt (Aris & Phillips, 1980)

Toby A. H. Wilkinson, Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge, 2001)

pointDescs.-2686: The Third Dynasty begins under Djoser, who orders the Step Pyramid at Saqqara; Imhotep develops building in stone.
pointDescs.-2613: Sneferu founds the Fourth Dynasty, holds territory from Libya to Sinai and Nubia, founds Buhen and builds three pyramids.
pointDescs.-2589: Khufu commissions the Great Pyramid of Giza; the fully developed pyramid style is reached.
pointDescs.-2558: Khafre, after a possible quarrel with his brother Djedefre, builds the second pyramid of Giza and, in traditional thinking, the Great Sphinx.
pointDescs.-2532: Menkaure builds the smallest of the three great pyramids of Giza; expeditions reach into Canaan and Nubia.
pointDescs.-2494: Userkaf founds the Fifth Dynasty; the cult of Ra grows and sun temples rise at Abusir.
pointDescs.-2487: Sahure commands an expedition to Punt; Egyptian ships trade for cedar in Lebanon and sail the Red Sea.
pointDescs.-2375: Unas has the Pyramid Texts inscribed in his pyramid, the first king to do so.
pointDescs.-2345: The Sixth Dynasty begins; under Pepi I and Merenre I trade flourishes and armies campaign in Nubia and Canaan, while the nomarchs grow powerful.
pointDescs.-2300: The canal to Lake Moeris is dug, a very large work of Nile flood control.
pointDescs.-2278: Pepi II begins his long reign; internal disorders set in towards its end.
pointDescs.-2214: Pepi II dies, well after his intended heirs; succession struggles follow and civil war comes within decades.
pointDescs.-2200: Drought cuts rainfall, and for some years between 2200 and 2150 BCE the Nile fails to flood.
pointDescs.-2181: The Sixth Dynasty ends; famine and strife open the First Intermediate Period.

notes: The article gives the Old Kingdom as c. 2700–c. 2200 BC in its lede and 2686–2181 BC (Third to Sixth Dynasty) in its body; the register follows the latter.
Djoser's own dates are 'sometime between 2691 and 2625 BC'; the -2686 point and the first event use the Third Dynasty's start.
The article does not date Pepi I or Merenre I; their reigns are placed at the dynasty's start (-2345).
The 2025 genome study is given in one sentence; its detailed percentages and models are left out.
